sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Neptūnus** (*neptunus*) — The Lord of Waters — belongs to the Roman tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sea, Horses, Earthquake". The name means "Possibly related to nepos (descendant) or a pre-Roman water root"[^1].

Neptūnus was god of fresh water before he was god of the sea: his oldest festival, the Neptunalia, falls in the parching days of late July, when Romans built huts of branches and prayed the waters not to fail. The Greek sea came later, and with it Poseidṓn's whole mythology.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Neptūnus** and serves its temple at [neptūnus.com](https://xn--neptnus-3sb.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *neptunus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.
Horace, Carmina / Opera, Oxford Classical Texts; Loeb, 23 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Neptūnus** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "Possibly related to nepos (descendant) or a pre-Roman water root"[^1].

The ASCII form *neptunus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Neptūnus** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **n** → **N** — Same letter
- **e** → **e** — Same letter
- **p** → **p** — Same letter
- **t** → **t** — Same letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **s** → **s** — Same letter

The project holds the domain **neptūnus.com** (xn--neptnus-3sb.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro), Aeneid / Eclogues / Georgics, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 19 BCE.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/nepˈtuː.nus/** — Classical Latin.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: nep-TOO-nus, long ū on the stressed second syllable.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Latin** — Neptūnus
- **Greek twin** — Ποσειδῶν
- **Etruscan** — Nethuns
- **Owned form** — Neptūnus

The etymology of Neptūnus is genuinely uncertain: the Etruscan sea god Nethuns stands behind him, and linguists have proposed a pre-Indo-European Mediterranean origin, with Pokorny suggesting a root for "damp, wet." The long ū of the second syllable is the secure classical quantity — the macron marks it in the restoration.

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.body:
The original script for this roman name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Neptūnus** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Neptūnus was god of fresh water before he was god of the sea: his oldest festival, the Neptunalia, falls in the parching days of late July, when Romans built huts of branches and prayed the waters not to fail. The Greek sea came later, and with it Poseidṓn's whole mythology.[^1]

### The Trident

The three-pronged fisher's spear that became the sceptre of the sea — and of a planet.

### Neptunus Equester

His Roman title as horse-lord: the consus-cult of underground granaries and racing.

### The Earth-Shaker

Ennosigaios in Greek, but Rome knew him too — the power that moves the ground the city stands on.

### Neptunalia

July 23: arbours of woven branches, water rites at the height of the drought.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Neptūnus concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The trident** — The fisher's tool exalted to kingship of three water-realms
- **The horse** — His second domain — waves and stallions share one crest
- **The dolphin** — His messenger and the sailor's friend

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Rome gave Neptūnus few native myths — his biography is Poseidṓn's translated — but the festival and the horse-cult are Italy's own, older than the sea-borrowing.[^1]

### The Huts of Branches (The Drought)

The Neptunalia of July 23 is Rome's oldest water rite: families built umbrae — huts woven of leafy branches — and poured water offerings at the height of summer's drought. The god's first realm was the spring and the stream, the waters that keep a farm alive; the Mediterranean, with its trade and war, was the empire's later gift to him.[^2]

### Lord of the Race (The Horse)

As Neptunus Equester he shared the underground altar of Consus, god of stored grain, at whose games — the Consualia — horses and mules were garlanded and rested from labour. It was at one such festival that Romulus staged the seizure of the Sabine women: Rome's foundation story begins at Neptūnus' racetrack, with the horses watching.

### Minerva and the City (The Contest)

Roman retellings kept the Greek contest for Athens: Neptūnus struck the Acropolis with his trident and brought forth the salt spring — or the first horse — but Minerva's olive won the city's name. The myth explained, for Roman readers, why wisdom outranks force: a civic lesson the conquerors of the Mediterranean repeated against themselves.

### Agrippa at Naulochus (The Plea)

When Agrippa destroyed Sextus Pompeius' fleet at Naulochus in 36 BCE, the victory was dedicated to Neptune — and the poet Horace marked the sea-god's favour to the Julian cause. Roman sea-power, relatively late in coming, made the borrowed god genuinely Roman: by the empire, Neptūnus had sailors' cults from Ostia to the British coast.

sources.citation: Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.
Horace, Carmina / Opera, Oxford Classical Texts; Loeb, 23 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
His equation with Poseidṓn is one of the oldest certain interpretatio Romana; his Etruscan substrate Nethuns appears on the Piacenza liver, the bronze model used to read omens. In the provinces he fused with local water powers — the Celtic river gods of Gaul and the Germanic North Sea powers — and his name became the standard gloss for "whatever god rules deep water here."[^1]

Within the Roman tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[diana|Diāna]], [[ianus|Iānus]], [[iuno|Iūnō]], [[iuppiter|Iūppiter]], [[vulcanus|Vulcānus]], and [[aseratu|Ašeratu]].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: The planet Neptune — discovered by mathematics before telescopes (Adams and Le Verrier, 1846) — carries his name and trident symbol into every classroom. "Neptune's realm" is still navy slang for the open sea; the Order of Neptune initiates sailors crossing the equator; and the trident survives from Ukrainian heraldry to Maserati's badge. Every western image of the sea as a person is his portrait.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The Piacenza liver (3rd–2nd century BCE) inscribes Nethuns on the liver's sea-zone — the Etruscan original caught in bronze. His Roman temple stood by the Circus Flaminius; the great marine-thiasos mosaics of North Africa and Ostia show the imperial image: the god in his hippocamp chariot. In Britain, the curse tablets of Bath and the altar of the Classis Britannica at Boulogne record sailors' vows to Neptune across the empire's wet edge.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
His Roman titles keep the memory of the land-water god under the sea-god.

- **Equester** — 'of the Horses'; his cult title at the Circus altar, shared with Consus.
- **Pelagius** — 'of the Open Sea'; the sea-faring title of the empire's sailors.
- **Ennosigaios** — 'Earth-Shaker'; Poseidṓn's Homeric title, translated and kept.
- **Pater** — 'the Father'; the old Italic water-father of the springs.
- **Dominus maris** — 'lord of the sea'; the imperial poets' full style.

sources.citation: Varro and Festus on Neptunus Equester; Horace, Odes 1.5.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: His Roman temple stood by the **Circus Flaminius**, restored under the empire and tied to the horse-cult of the Consualia; the Neptunalia arbours of July 23 filled the fields around it. At **Ostia**, the harbour city's sailors kept his cult in the corporations' clubhouses, and the great marine mosaics of the baths show his thiasos exactly as the sailors imagined him. In the provinces his altars line the sea-roads: the Boulogne altar of the Classis Britannica and the curse-tablets of Britain's waters record the empire's vows to the god of crossings.

sources.citation: The Ostia mosaic corpora; CIL XIII (Boulogne altar).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Neptūnus began as the water that must be prayed for and became the water that must be crossed. He holds both truths: the sea that feeds and the sea that swallows, the spring in the drought and the earthquake under the harbour. To sail, to drill a well, to trust the ground — each is a small treaty with him.

The drought-festival and the sea-empire belong together, and the old god keeps both books still: the water we pray for and the water we fear, the well and the wave. Every age that pumps an aquifer or insures a coastline is doing his liturgy in engineering — asking the question his festival asked in the July heat: will the water come, will it be enough, and what will it cost when it does?[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
